The desert woodrat (Neotoma lepida) is a medium-sized cricetid rodent that exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of species occupying arid and semi-arid environments across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Neonates are altricial at the time of parturition, with field measurements consistently documenting a wet weight at birth of 8.45 grams [Wwb = 8.45 grams]. This relatively modest birth mass, typical of small-bodied rodents, is followed by a period of rapid growth during the suckling juvenile stage. The developing young rely entirely on maternal milk for nutritional support, and the duration of this dependency is tightly regulated by physiological constraints. Under the standard thermal conditions typical of a gestating female's core body temperature (36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]), the gestation period has been recorded to last 33 days [tg = 33 days], which aligns closely with values reported for other members of the genus Neotoma. This relatively short intrauterine development period reflects a reproductive strategy that prioritizes rapid offspring production in response to unpredictable resource availability in desert ecosystems.

Following parturition, the pre-weaning period in Neotoma lepida is characterized by continued maternal investment through lactation. Detailed observational studies of captive colonies have determined that the time since birth at weaning is 31 days [tx = 31 days], measured under conditions held constant at 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. At this critical developmental milestone, the wet weight at weaning is typically recorded at 35 grams [Wwx = 35 grams], representing a more than fourfold increase from the neonatal mass. The weaned juvenile then enters a phase of independent foraging during which somatic growth proceeds steadily as the animal navigates its often harsh, xeric habitat. The transition to nutritional emancipation is a particularly vulnerable period for young woodrats, as they must simultaneously learn to identify palatable forage items, including toxic creosote bush (Larrea tridentata), and evade predation. Mortality during this juvenile stage is substantial, and only a fraction of the cohort survives to reach the pubertal transition.

Sexual maturation in female desert woodrats follows a predictable schedule that is cued by a combination of photoperiod, nutritional condition, and body size rather than solely by chronological age. Under the consistent thermal regime of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C] maintained in laboratory breeding studies, the time since birth at puberty for females was observed to be 76 days [tp = 76 days]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capacity is a common life-history strategy among small desert mammals that face short windows of favorable breeding conditions. The ultimate wet weight of a sexually mature adult female approaches 236 grams [Wwi = 236 grams], though males may achieve slightly larger dimensions in some populations. This body mass represents the species' maximum recorded somatic investment, and it is typically achieved well after sexual maturity has been reached. The disparity in timing between the onset of gonadal activity and the attainment of final mass underscores the importance of continued somatic growth for reproductive success in a competitive, resource-limited environment.

Females of Neotoma lepida exhibit a moderately high reproductive output that is characteristic of species with pronounced r-selected life-history strategies. In the wild, the maximum reproductive rate is achieved at a body temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C], reflecting the elevated metabolic demands associated with intense reproductive effort. Litter sizes are modest, with females producing 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 pups per litter], a value consistent across most of the species' geographic range. Under optimal resource conditions, which typically coincide with the mild temperatures and increased rainfall of spring, breeding females can initiate up to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 3 litters per year]. This combination of litter size and litter frequency allows the species to rapidly capitalize on ephemeral resource pulses, converting abundant food into new recruits before environmental conditions deteriorate again. The energetic cost of lactation places substantial physiological strain on the dam, however, and consecutive litters may be spaced further apart during periods of drought or food scarcity.

The maximum lifespan recorded for desert woodrats in their natural environment is a reflection of their position in the desert food web. Under field conditions at an average core temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], maximum longevity has been estimated at approximately 10.5 years [am = approximately 10.5 years]. This figure, derived from mark-recapture studies in the Mojave Desert, is relatively substantial for a rodent of this body size and likely reflects the protective benefits of their large, elaborately constructed middens, which provide refuge from both thermal extremes and predators. The species plays a significant ecological role in its community, as the woodrat's caches of plant material create microhabitats utilized by arthropods, reptiles, and other small mammals. Ultimately, senescence in older individuals is marked by a progressive deterioration of body condition, and most mortality in adults appears to be driven by predation from owls, snakes, and coyotes rather than by intrinsic physiological failure. Further comparative studies across the geographic range of Neotoma lepida would help clarify how variation in climate, resource availability, and predation pressure shapes the expression of these key life-history parameters.
